To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
propagule limitation, disparate habitat quality and variation in selection pressure may impede range expansion at a local species range boundary.

(1) habitat quality and phenotypic selection varied across a local species range boundary, and (2) the range margin exerted unique selection pressure, which was not intermediate between core habitat and exterior habitat.

(1) habitat quality declines sharply across the local range boundary of G. tricolor, (2) some migrants are able to establish in suitable sites at and beyond the population boundary, (3) phenotypic selection varies across habitats, and (4) the habitat at the range boundary often exerts unique selection pressures.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of ecological processes in limiting range shifts in the face of climate change, with a focus on the importance of variation in propagule supply and habitat quality, and the role of spatial heterogeneity in natural selection.
how the spatial heterogeneity of selection pressures influences the evolution and ecology of species range boundaries.
the role of ecological and evolutionary processes in shaping the distribution and abundance of species, and the potential for species to respond to changing environmental conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the combination of propagule limitation, disparate habitat quality, and variation in phenotypic natural selection at a local species range boundary may impede adaptive range expansion, and that these processes should be considered when assessing species range limits and the potential for range shifts under global change scenarios.
propagule limitation and variation in habitat quality at the edge of a population range may reduce opportunities for range expansion, even over short distances.
the combination of propagule limitation, spatially varying habitat quality, and heterogeneous selection may limit opportunities for adaptive range expansions, even over short distances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the range boundary of G. tricolor in the Mojave Desert is a dynamic, spatially heterogeneous mosaic of suitable and unsuitable habitats that is not simply an ecotone between core habitat and the surrounding matrix of unsuitable habitat, and that selection on plant traits is heterogeneous across the landscape.
the combination of propagule limitation, spatial variation in habitat quality (and thus in fitness) and selection on phenotypes can limit the range of species.
range boundaries are not static, but are dynamic, and that they may be influenced by a combination of ecological, genetic and evolutionary forces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
range expansions are not necessarily straightforward processes.
the ecological dynamics of range margins are complex and may not always be predictable from patterns of habitat quality or selection within the core of the species range.
the local range margin is not a simple transition between core and exterior habitat conditions.
